passage: A familiar way of thinking about Western art music divides the creative labour with reassuring neatness. The composer makes the work and records it in a score; the performer's task is to realise the score faithfully, adding as little of himself as the music allows. On this view the score is the work, or at least its complete specification, and a performance is good to the degree that it delivers what the notation contains. Its attractions are considerable. It accounts for our confidence that two strikingly different performances are nevertheless performances of the same composition, and it furnishes the critic with a standard: the performer who alters the notes has made a mistake, whatever the result sounds like.

The difficulty is that notation specifies far less than the view requires. A score fixes pitches and their order with considerable precision, and durations rather less, but a great deal of what listeners hear as the character of a performance is left open or indicated only roughly. A marking that asks for a loud passage does not say how loud, and the right loudness in a small room is not the right loudness in a large hall. A word indicating a lively tempo admits a range of speeds wide enough to make one performance sound urgent and another relaxed. Nothing in the marks tells the player exactly how long to linger at the high point of a phrase, or how to weigh the notes of a chord against one another. These are not trivial details that a faithful performer can safely settle at random; they are much of what makes the music sound the way it does.

One response is to swing to the opposite extreme and say that the work simply is the performance, the score being no more than a set of instructions that each performer completes as she pleases. This rescues the performer's creative contribution, but at a considerable theoretical price. It cannot explain why some performances strike informed listeners as wrong-headed even when every note is in place, or why a performer who takes a slow movement at double speed has done something worse than make an unusual choice. If the score were merely a recipe to be finished at will, there would be no ground for such judgements, and yet musicians make them constantly and with considerable agreement.

That agreement points to what both positions conspicuously omit. Scores are never interpreted in isolation. They are read by musicians trained in a practice: a shared and largely unwritten understanding of what the marks mean in a given style, which conventions apply, what kinds of freedom are expected and where those freedoms stop. In music of one period a trill is understood to begin on the note above; in another it begins on the main note; the score is usually silent on the point, and the practice supplies the answer. The work, on this account, is neither the marks alone nor whatever a given performance makes of them, but the marks as a practice reads them. Fidelity is owed to that combination.

It may be objected that practices evolve, so that the work would apparently evolve with them, which seems absurd. But the objection establishes considerably less than it appears to. Practices do change, slowly, and the identity of a work is correspondingly less fixed than the first view supposed; that is a cost worth accepting, since it matches how musicians actually argue about performances. What does not follow is that anything goes. A practice at any moment draws lines that its members can defend, and a performer who knowingly crosses them is making a claim that must be argued for, not exercising a right.

options.C: been accurate to the marks on the page without being faithful to the work they belong to.
options.D: created a new work, because a work changes whenever the practice used to read its score changes.

passage: For much of the last century it was an article of faith among progressive architects that ornament was a kind of lie. A building, they argued, should declare its structure and its purpose plainly; carving and moulding added cost without adding use, and they disguised what a building really was beneath a costume borrowed from some other age. The argument had moral force, and it produced buildings of great clarity. It also rested on a narrow idea of what counts as use.

Consider what ornament has traditionally done: a carved surround tells a stranger which of many openings is the entrance, so that nobody needs to read a sign to find the way in. A band of moulding at the level of the first floor breaks a tall wall into parts that a human eye can measure, so that a passer-by senses the height of the building in storeys rather than as an undifferentiated cliff. Projecting mouldings over windows throw rain clear of the glass and, as they weather, gather their stains in a pattern that reads as intended rather than as decay. Even purely figurative ornament, a row of leaves or a face above a door, offers the eye something to rest on at walking pace, which is the pace at which most people meet most buildings. These are uses, though not of the kind that appear in a structural calculation.

The critics were right about one thing: ornament applied without regard to any of these purposes, stuck on to a facade like a label on a jar, is as dishonest as they said, and much commercial building of their day was exactly that. But the remedy they chose, to strip surfaces bare, threw away the work along with the pretence. A blank wall is not neutral, for it tells the stranger nothing about where to go in, it offers no measure of scale, and it weathers into streaks that look like neglect because nothing in its design anticipated them. The plain building is honest about its structure and silent about almost everything else that a person on the street needs to know.

The more useful question, then, is not whether a building should be ornamented but what its ornament is for. Asked in that way, the question rules out a good deal of pastiche, the reproduction of historical detail for its associations alone. It also rules out a good deal of austerity that passes itself off as rigour, and it returns the judgement of a facade to the people who have to find their way past it.

passage: Few moral injunctions are now repeated with more confidence than the injunction to remember. After a civil war, a dictatorship or a period of communal violence, it is taken almost for granted that the truth must be told, the dead named and the guilty identified, and that a society which declines to do so is building its future on a lie. The case for this view is strong, and nothing that follows is meant to deny it. Those who suffered have a claim to be believed, and a society that teaches its children a false account of its own recent past does them a lasting harm. But the view carries an assumption that deserves examination: that remembering, in public and in detail, is always what allows former enemies to go on living side by side.

The historical record is less obliging than the injunction. A number of societies, ancient and modern, have made peace by agreeing, in one form or another, not to reopen the wrongs of the conflict just ended. Such agreements are often described as attempts at forgetting, but the description is misleading. No decree can make people forget what they suffered or what they did, and none of these arrangements tried to. What they established was something narrower: a rule about the public use of the past. Past crimes would not be prosecuted, or not beyond a certain point; old grievances would not be made the basis of political campaigns; the question of who had done what to whom would, for a time, be kept out of the courts and the assemblies, even as it continued to be remembered in kitchens and graveyards.

Whether such a rule is wise seems to depend less on the principle involved than on timing. In the first years after a conflict, when the losing side still has the means to fight and the institutions of the new order are fragile, a full public reckoning may reopen the war it is meant to close, and the people most likely to pay for that are the ones a reckoning was supposed to vindicate. A generation later, the balance may look quite different. The armed men have grown old, the institutions have settled, and the children of those who suffered may reasonably ask why the silence that once protected the peace should still protect those who did the harm.

For the costs of silence do not fall evenly. The perpetrator who is spared prosecution gains something definite; the victim who is asked not to speak of what was done gives something up, and is often asked to do so by people who lost far less. A peace that rests indefinitely on such an asymmetry is unlikely to remain a peace in any full sense. It may endure as an arrangement while decaying as a settlement, leaving resentments that later politicians find all too easy to exploit.

The upshot is that agreed silence should be judged neither as a betrayal of memory nor as a model of wisdom, but as a provisional arrangement whose legitimacy depends on what happens to it later. A silence that a society chooses, and later chooses to break, may have served both peace and justice in their turn. The worst outcome is not silence as such but a silence that becomes permanent by default, that no one ever decides to keep, and that is mistaken, by those who benefit from it, for a consensus that was never actually reached.

passage: The word 'stress' entered the study of living things from the study of materials, where its meaning is reasonably exact: the internal force per unit area within a body subjected to a load. In engineering, stress is distinguished from strain, the deformation that the load produces, and both are distinguished from the load itself. When the word was borrowed to describe what happens to organisms under pressure, these distinctions did not travel with it. In ordinary speech, and in a good deal of research, 'stress' can refer to the demanding situation, to the bodily and emotional reaction it provokes, or to the relation between the two, and it is often far from clear which of these is meant. A survey announcing that most workers feel stressed may be measuring their workloads, their symptoms or their sense of being overwhelmed, and the headline rarely says which.

The slippage is not merely a matter of untidy usage. Consider the familiar claim that stress is bad for health. If stress means the reaction, and the reaction is defined partly by its harmful effects, the claim is close to true by definition. If stress means the demanding situation, the claim is plainly false as a generalisation, since many people meet heavy demands without harm and some appear to thrive on them. Only if stress means a particular relation, demands that exceed what a person believes they can manage, does the claim become a substantive hypothesis that could turn out to be wrong. Much popular discussion moves among these meanings without noticing, and so acquires the authority of the first reading and the scope of the second.

The same confusion shadows the more recent enthusiasm for 'good stress'. To say that some stress is beneficial may mean that some demanding situations are worth seeking out, which is uncontroversial; or that some physiological reactions to demand improve performance, which is plausible within limits; or that people who interpret their reactions as helpful fare better than those who do not, which is a specific claim requiring specific evidence. Advice built on the phrase often slides from the first meaning, which everyone accepts, to the third, which is the one actually being sold. Each of the three deserves to be judged on its own evidence, and the plausibility of the first lends nothing to the third.

It might seem that the remedy is to abandon the word altogether. That would be a mistake, and not only because ordinary language is not so easily reformed. The very breadth of the term has allowed researchers in physiology, psychology, sociology and medicine to recognise that they were studying related things, and it has drawn attention to connections, between working conditions and heart disease, say, that narrower vocabularies might have kept apart. Whole programmes of research, on bereavement, on unemployment, on the burdens of caring for a sick relative, found a common frame in it. A concept can be scientifically fruitful precisely because it is loose at the edges, so long as those who use it know where the looseness lies.

What the word cannot do is carry an argument by itself. The useful discipline is to ask, whenever a claim about stress is made, which of its meanings is in play, and whether the evidence offered supports the claim under that meaning or only under a different one. A finding about reactions does not automatically license advice about situations, and a finding about interpretations says little about either. Keeping the senses apart costs a few extra words; failing to keep them apart has cost a good deal of confusion, some of it in the very places where clarity matters most.

passage: Among the records of past climate, ice cores enjoy a special prestige. Drilled from the great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, they contain small bubbles of air sealed off as snow was buried and compressed, so that a scientist can, in a sense, hold in a laboratory a sample of the atmosphere as it was long before any human being farmed. Tree rings, lake sediments and the shells of tiny marine organisms all have to be translated into climate through some chain of reasoning. The bubbles in ice seem to need no translation at all: the gas is simply there, waiting to be measured.

The appearance of directness is partly an illusion, and an instructive one. Snow does not seal itself the moment it falls. For decades, centuries or, at the driest sites, far longer, depending on how quickly snow accumulates, the upper layer remains porous, and air from the surface continues to mix downward through it. By the time the bubbles finally close, the gas they hold is considerably younger than the ice that surrounds it. To date the air, then, researchers must model how compaction proceeds at a given site, which in turn depends on temperature and snowfall, the very quantities the core is being used to reconstruct. Temperature itself is not read off the ice but inferred from the proportions of heavier and lighter forms of water, a relationship calibrated against modern observations and assumed to have held in the past.

None of this makes the records untrustworthy. It does, however, change where their authority comes from. A core is persuasive not because it bypasses interpretation but because its interpretations can be checked against one another and against independent archives. Traces of very large volcanic eruptions, which can appear in cores drilled at opposite ends of the planet, allow records to be aligned; the timing of changes in ice can be compared with changes recorded in ocean sediments, whose dating rests on quite different assumptions. When such independent lines agree, the agreement is far harder to explain away than any single measurement, however direct it seems.

The point matters beyond the laboratory. Public arguments about climate often treat evidence as either raw and therefore reliable or interpreted and therefore suspect. Ice cores show why this division is unhelpful. Almost all scientific evidence is interpreted; what distinguishes strong evidence from weak is whether its interpretations are exposed to independent tests that could have failed. A measurement trusted because it seemed to speak for itself would deserve less confidence than one whose inferences had been stated openly and checked.

passage: An investigation that changes a law or ends a career is remembered for its result, and the result makes it look like a sound investment. The reporting behind it rarely looks that way while it is under way. A team may spend months requesting documents, cultivating reluctant sources and checking figures, only to discover at the end that the story cannot be stood up, or that it is smaller and duller than it seemed. No publication can know in advance which of its inquiries will succeed, so the cost of the one that does must also cover the many that quietly fail. Editors who have watched a promising inquiry collapse after half a year learn caution, and caution, in a publication under financial pressure, usually means fewer inquiries.

This uncertainty would matter less if the rewards of success flowed back to the publication that paid for it. Mostly they do not. Once a finding is published, rivals can report it within hours, and the citizens who benefit from a cleaner tendering process or a safer bridge are seldom the readers who bought the paper that exposed the problem. In the language economists use, the work produces benefits that spill over to people who did not pay for them, and goods of that kind tend to be supplied in smaller quantities than a society, if it could choose collectively, would want.

The most important of those benefits is also the least visible. Officials who know that their accounts might one day be examined behave differently from officials who are sure that they will not be. A local administration that expects a reporter to read its contracts has a reason to keep them clean, and the corruption that never takes place leaves no story behind it. The contractor who decides not to inflate an invoice, because a reporter once asked awkward questions about a neighbouring council, will never appear in any account of what journalism has achieved. Investigative journalism therefore works partly as a deterrent, and like other deterrents it is judged unfairly by its visible output; a quiet year may be evidence of its success rather than of its irrelevance.

Admirers of the form sometimes overstate its virtues. Investigations can be mistaken, and a reporter convinced of wrongdoing may read ambiguous evidence in only one direction, with real costs for the people named. Nor is every exposure a public service; some are driven more by rivalry or an appetite for scandal than by any public interest. But the case for supporting such work does not depend on its infallibility. It depends on presence. Deterrence works only if the possibility of scrutiny is continuous; a single celebrated exposure every decade, however brilliant, does less to discipline the powerful than a modest but permanent habit of looking. Those who fund journalism, whether readers, donors or the public purse, should therefore value a steady capacity for inquiry above the occasional prize-winning scoop.

passage: We tend to judge a portrait by asking whether it captures the person. A good portrait, on this view, reveals something of the sitter's inner life: a habit of mind, a private sorrow, the particular way one face differs from all others. Measured against this standard, many older portraits seem stiff and oddly impersonal. Rows of nobles stand in nearly identical poses, their faces composed into the same calm, their individuality apparently buried beneath velvet and armour. It is easy to conclude that their painters were trying to capture the person and largely failing.

That conclusion mistakes what such portraits were for. For much of the history of European portraiture, and of several other traditions, the purpose of a commissioned portrait was less to record a personality than to establish a position. The sitter appeared as a holder of office, an heir, a bride, the head of a house. Costume, setting and objects carried meanings that contemporaries could read: the chain of a civic office, a dog standing for fidelity, a column suggesting constancy, a distant estate glimpsed through a window. A portrait of this kind was closer to a document than to a confession. Its sameness was not a failure of observation but a deliberate placing of the individual within a recognisable type, since what the patron wished to have recorded was precisely the type he had come to occupy. A contemporary who knew the conventions could read an entire biography of rank in a single canvas, whereas a modern viewer expecting the revelation of a character finds only an inventory of possessions.

Likeness was not irrelevant. Families wanted to know what an absent bride looked like, and painters could be criticised for flattering too much or too little. But likeness served the larger purpose rather than defining it. A face had to be recognisable enough to attach the role to the right person, and beyond that the painter's task was to make the person fit the role. The expectation that a portrait should instead expose the sitter, catching him off guard or revealing what he might prefer to hide, belongs to a later and narrower moment in the genre's history. Where an older portrait does strike modern eyes as startlingly intimate, it is worth asking whether it was made for a public hall or for a private room, since the obligations of display weighed very differently in the two settings.

Several changes made that expectation possible. The growth of a buying public outside courts and great houses created sitters with no office to display. New ideas about the self encouraged the belief that a person's truth lay within rather than in his station. And when photography arrived in the nineteenth century, it soon took over much of the trade in cheap likenesses, leaving painters free, or obliged, to offer something a camera seemed unable to supply. The psychological portrait, in other words, is not the essence of the genre finally achieved but one of its historical forms.

To say this is not to claim that the older portraits had no inner life, or that modern ones are free of display. A shrewd painter could let a sitter's character show through the conventions, and a present-day portrait of a company chairman, with its carefully chosen office and posture, documents a position as surely as any court painting did. The point is only that we should judge a portrait by the question it was asked to answer. Faulting a court painter for failing to reveal a soul is like faulting a map for failing to be a landscape painting.

passage: Translators of the great books of the past often remark on a puzzle. The original of an old epic or a classical tragedy does not seem to age; readers return to it century after century and find it as alive as ever. Yet translations of the same work date quickly. A version that seemed fresh to its first readers can sound stiff or quaint within a lifetime, and every generation or two a new one appears, prefaced by the claim that its predecessors have become unreadable. Why should the copy age when the original, which is older and in many ways stranger, does not? The question is worth more attention than it usually receives, because the answer says something about what a translation is.

The usual answer is linguistic: a translation is written in the language of its own moment, with that moment's idioms and its notions of what sounds dignified and what sounds plain, and these change. The original, by contrast, has been absorbed into a tradition that reads it as a historical text and forgives its strangeness. There is truth in this, but it cannot be the whole story, since old translations are often perfectly intelligible and still feel inadequate.

A deeper reason lies in what translation requires. A great work is full of places where its sense is undecided: a word that could mean anger or grief, a line whose tone could be mocking or tender, a scene whose moral weight is left to the reader. The original can leave such places open, and much of its power to sustain rereading comes from that openness; a translator has no such freedom, because writing in another language forces choices at every point, and each choice settles a question the original left unsettled. The choices are not arbitrary, but they are shaped by what the translator's own age finds plausible or important, and so the translation records one generation's reading of the work. When the concerns of that generation fade, its translation comes to look like what it always was: an interpretation.

Seen in this light, retranslation is not a sign that earlier translators failed. It is one of the ways a classic stays alive, each version making a fresh set of decisions and so showing a new reader something the others concealed. There is even an occasional reversal. Some translations become works of literature in their own right, read not as windows onto the original but for their own sake, and these, curiously, stop ageing in the way translations usually do; they come to be read, like originals, as historical texts. Their choices no longer look like a period's reading of another book; they look like the permanent features of a book of their own.

passage: Whenever a machine produces fluent language, the question returns of whether it understands what it says. Two answers dominate. One holds that understanding is shown in behaviour: if a system answers questions, follows instructions and sustains a conversation in ways we cannot distinguish from a competent person, there is nothing further we could reasonably ask of it, and to withhold the word is mere prejudice in favour of our own kind. The other holds that behaviour, however impressive, can be produced by manipulating symbols whose connection to the world the system never grasps, and that understanding requires something behind the performance, some grounding of words in perception, action or experience.

The two camps disagree about almost everything except one assumption, and that shared assumption is where the trouble lies. Both treat understanding as a single property that a system either has or lacks, so that the only task is to decide which side of the line it falls on. Yet when we attribute understanding to people we do nothing of the kind. A student may understand a theorem well enough to apply it to textbook problems but not well enough to see why it fails when one condition is dropped; a mechanic may understand an engine thoroughly in practice while being unable to explain its thermodynamics. We judge understanding by a battery of loosely connected abilities: explaining, extending to unfamiliar cases, noticing one's own mistakes, connecting what one knows to what one does. These abilities can come apart, and people possess them in very different measures.

If understanding is a cluster of this kind, the all-or-nothing question about machines is badly posed. A system may display some of the abilities to a high degree and others hardly at all; it may extend a pattern brilliantly in one domain and fail, without any sign of noticing, at a trivial variation in another. Saying that it 'really understands' flattens this profile into a verdict that tells us little, and saying that it 'merely manipulates symbols' does the same in the opposite direction. The useful work lies in mapping which abilities are present, under what conditions, and how robustly.

This proposal will not satisfy everyone. Someone who believes that understanding involves an inner experience of meaning will say that mapping abilities, however finely, leaves the essential question untouched. Perhaps it does. But that question, whatever its answer, is a question about experience, and it arises equally for any being whose inner life we cannot inspect. It should not be allowed to stand in for the more tractable question of what a system can and cannot reliably do, which is, after all, the question on which most practical decisions about such systems depend.

passage: A familiar story about civic life holds that ordinary people have withdrawn from it. Where their grandparents joined lodges, unions, parents' associations and choral societies, attended meetings and stood for office in them, people today are said to stay at home, absorbed in private amusements and too busy or too distrustful to join anything. The story is usually told as a matter of individual choice and individual failing, and the remedies proposed follow naturally from it: people should be encouraged, shamed or gently nudged back into joining.

There is another way to read much of the same evidence. What has declined is not association as such but a particular form of it: the federation of local branches, each with its own officers, meetings and dues, linked through elected delegates to regional and national bodies. In its place, many of the organisations that now claim to speak for citizens are run by professional staff from a central office. They recruit supporters through mailing lists and advertisements, ask them for money rather than time, and consult them, if at all, through surveys. Their membership lists may be long, but a member is someone who has made a payment, not someone who has attended a meeting, and nothing in the organisation's routine requires that members ever meet one another.

Read this way, the decline is less a withdrawal from below than a transformation from above. Organisations discovered that it was cheaper and more effective, at least for the purposes of lobbying and publicity, to raise money from many distant supporters than to sustain an expensive structure of local branches with their own halls, officers and opinions. Funders, too, preferred bodies with a clear national voice and a small, accountable staff, and the habits of professional management spread from one organisation to the next. The people who drifted away from the older associations may not have rejected participation at all; they may simply have been offered fewer occasions for it.

The distinction matters because the federated association did something its successors do not. It taught people with no political ambitions how to run a meeting, keep minutes, manage a budget, argue for a motion and accept defeat when it was voted down. These were not trivial accomplishments; they were the ordinary apprenticeship of democratic citizenship for many who would never hold public office. It also tied the local to the national: a member in a small town could, through a chain of elected representatives, influence what the national body did. A donor to a professionally managed organisation may support its aims with real conviction, but she learns none of these skills and holds no comparable thread of influence over what is done in her name.

It would be easy to turn this into nostalgia, and nostalgia would mislead. Many of the old associations excluded women or people of the wrong background, and their local meetings could be stifling and petty. The new organisations, for their part, have often been more effective at changing laws. Nor have people stopped gathering; they form online groups and informal networks with remarkable ease. But these are seldom built to govern themselves through elected officers and binding votes. If the loss is real, it is the loss of a school of self-government, and it will not be repaired by urging individuals to join more. It would require organisations to find reasons, and funders to give them reasons, to want members who turn up.

options.A: The decline of membership associations reflects organisations' choices about cheaper ways of raising money rather than any change in what ordinary people want.
options.B: Civic life has collapsed because people now prefer private amusements to the meetings and offices that earlier generations valued.
options.C: The fall in civic membership owes more to how organisations were rebuilt than to individual withdrawal, and it has cost citizens practice in governing themselves.
options.D: Professionally managed organisations are less legitimate than federations because they change laws without consulting their members.

passage: Many of the long novels of the nineteenth century first reached their readers not as books but in instalments, issued monthly or weekly over a year or more, in magazines or in separate parts. Modern criticism has tended to treat this fact as an extenuating circumstance. When such a novel sprawls, introduces a character it later forgets, or closes a chapter on a contrived moment of suspense, the serial is invoked as an excuse: the author was writing to deadline, paid by length, obliged to bring readers back next month. The implication is that the real novel, the one the author would have written in better conditions, lies somewhere beneath the one we have, and that serial publication is a kind of noise to be filtered out.

The trouble with this view is that it treats the serial only as a set of pressures, when it was also a set of possibilities, and many of the qualities we now admire in these books grew from it. A novel read over eighteen months is lived with in a way that a novel read over a week is not. Its characters age alongside their readers; its crises arrive amid the readers' own. The large casts and interwoven plots that later critics found unwieldy were in part a response to this rhythm, since a reader returning after a month's absence needed several lines of interest to pick up, and recurring figures with distinctive habits of speech helped her find her place. What looks in a single volume like digression could, at the pace of first reading, serve as the texture of a world one returned to.

Serial publication also made the novel unusually public while it was still unfinished. An instalment could be discussed before the next was written, and authors could, and sometimes did, adjust their plans in light of how readers responded. A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control. It can as easily be seen as a kind of conversation, in which a book took shape partly through its encounter with an audience rather than being delivered complete to readers whose only role was to receive it. For a time the novel became a shared event, followed by readers who knew that a great many others were reading the same pages in the same weeks.

None of this is to deny the costs. Writing to fixed lengths did produce padding, and the demand for suspense at the end of each part did produce cliffhangers that the story did not need and that read awkwardly once the parts were bound together. A reader of the collected volume is entitled to notice these. What deserves suspicion is the standard against which they are judged as failures: the ideal of the novel as a single, unified design, conceived whole and executed according to plan. That ideal has a history of its own, and it gained much of its authority later, among writers and critics who worked for a different market and under different conditions. Applied backward, it does not so much reveal the faults of serial fiction as convert its differences into faults.

There is, finally, an irony in the critical embarrassment. Long television dramas, released in episodes and discussed between them, are now often praised by critics for the very qualities, the slow accumulation, the large cast, the sense of a world lived alongside, that the instalment novel was once thought to need excusing for. Nothing about the newer form proves the older one right, and a slack episode is no better for belonging to a celebrated series. But the shift in judgement suggests that what critics of the instalment novel took for timeless standards of form were, at least in part, the habits of one particular way of reading.

options.A: indifferent, since the author regards the question of control as irrelevant to a novel's merits.
options.B: even-handed, since the author grants it as one possible reading while offering an alternative that is equally reasonable.
options.C: contemptuous, since the author treats it as a confusion that no serious critic could still hold.
options.D: approving, since the author agrees that serial novelists gave up too much to their audiences.

passage: In most markets the price does the work of allocation. If more people want a good than there are units of it, the price rises until the excess disappears, and whoever is willing to pay the new price obtains the good. But there is a family of markets in which this mechanism cannot operate, because each side must choose the other. A university cannot simply admit whoever is willing to pay the most, nor can an applicant simply buy a place; a hospital hiring junior doctors cares which doctors it gets, and the doctors care which hospital they join. In such markets, sometimes called matching markets, a transaction requires mutual acceptance, and no single number can bring about a match that both sides want.

Left to themselves, matching markets tend to fail in characteristic ways. One is unravelling: because the strongest candidates are in demand, employers try to secure them by making offers earlier than their rivals, and the competition for earliness can push offers so far forward that they are made before anyone knows how good the candidates are. Another is congestion: when offers must be accepted or refused quickly, a candidate holding one offer may not learn in time of a better one, and the market clears without having considered all its possibilities. A third is strategic misrepresentation, in which participants conceal their true preferences, ranking a likely option first rather than the one they actually want, because they fear that revealing their real wishes will cost them.

The remedy that has often been adopted is not deregulation but construction: a clearinghouse to which both sides submit ranked lists, and which computes an assignment by a procedure known to have certain properties. The property most often sought is stability, meaning that there is no applicant and employer, not matched to each other, who would both prefer to be. A stable assignment removes the motive to break ranks, since no such pair can do better by striking a private deal, and with a suitable procedure at least one side can be given no reason to misreport its preferences. Such clearinghouses show that a market is not always a spontaneous order arising wherever people are free to trade; it can be an artefact, built to solve problems that freedom alone creates.

None of this means that design can substitute for the willingness of participants. A clearinghouse works only if enough of both sides join it, and an elegant procedure is useless if the most sought-after employers find it more profitable to recruit privately. Nor can a procedure deliver every desirable property at once: no procedure, for instance, can give both sides complete reason to report honestly while always producing stable outcomes. The designer chooses among imperfect options, and the choice reflects judgements about whose interests deserve protection. The engineering of markets is thus a political as well as a technical art, but it is an art that can be practised well or badly, and the difference matters to the people whose lives it arranges.

options.A: A prestigious hospital declines to join the clearinghouse and fills its posts by recruiting the doctors it wants privately.
options.B: A law firm, keen to secure the strongest graduates, makes its offers in their first year of study rather than their last.
options.C: A graduate accepts the only offer she holds because it must be answered within hours, and later learns of a better one.
options.D: In a ranked-list scheme for course places, a student puts a less popular course first, fearing that naming her favourite would lose her the safer place.

passage: A parable that became famous in the second half of the twentieth century asks us to imagine a pasture open to all. Each herder, reasoning that the benefit of an extra animal is his alone while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, adds another, and then another, until the grass is gone and all are ruined. The moral usually drawn is stark: resources held in common will be destroyed unless they are divided into private plots or placed under the control of the state.

The parable is persuasive, but it describes something that most actual commons are not. In many villages, pastures, woodlots, fishing ponds and irrigation channels have been shared for generations without being exhausted, and not because the villagers were unusually selfless. They were governed by rules. A household might be allowed to graze only as many animals as it could feed through the winter from its own fields; grazing might move between sections of the hill in a fixed rotation; a watchman, paid in grain, might patrol the boundary, and offenders might face fines that rose with each repeated offence. The herders of the parable have no such rules, no means of watching one another and no way of punishing those who cheat. What the parable describes is not a commons but open access, a resource that belongs to no community at all.

This does not mean that village commons always survive. They tend to fail in recognisable circumstances: when outsiders who are not bound by local rules can enter freely, when a distant authority overrides local arrangements with regulations that villagers neither understand nor respect, when migration thins the community so much that no one is left to keep watch, or when a sudden rise in the value of the resource makes cheating more tempting than it has ever been. These are real dangers. But they are dangers to particular institutions, not proof that shared ownership is doomed by human nature.

The practical lesson is that the familiar choice between private property and state control is too narrow. To say so is not to romanticise village life; such arrangements can be strict, and some are unequal, giving larger shares to households that hold more land. Even so, a third possibility, communities managing their own resources by rules they have made and can enforce, has a long record of success, and policy that ignores it may destroy working arrangements in the name of preventing a tragedy that was never going to happen.

options.A: a fair remedy for the inequality of village arrangements that give larger shares to households holding more land.
options.B: a risk to the commons if the villagers neither understand the new rules nor accept them as legitimate.
options.C: an unwelcome change, but one that cannot affect whether the commons survives, since that depends on human nature.
options.D: a safeguard the commons needs, since local rules cannot restrain households once the resource rises in value.

passage: For a time it was widely believed, among journalists and fact-checkers as much as among researchers, that correcting a false belief could make matters worse. The idea, which came to be called the backfire effect, held that people confronted with evidence against a cherished belief would not merely resist it but cling to the belief more tightly, as though the correction were an attack to be repelled. It had an intuitive appeal: most of us have argued with someone who seemed to grow more certain with every fact we offered. And it carried a discouraging moral. If correction backfires, perhaps it is better not to correct at all.

Subsequent research has been considerably kinder to correction. Larger studies, with more varied topics and more diverse participants, have generally found that people who receive a factual correction move, on average, towards the accurate view, even when the correction cuts against their political loyalties. Reversal of the kind the early findings described appears to be rare, and some of the original results have proved difficult to reproduce. The more careful conclusion is not that people are perfectly responsive to evidence but that they are responsive to it in the ordinary, imperfect way: they update, though often less than they should.

It is worth asking why the backfire idea spread so far on so slender a basis. Part of the answer is that it flattered a certain cynicism about the public, and part is that it confused resistance with reversal. Someone who hears a correction and does not change his mind has resisted it; someone who becomes more convinced of the falsehood has reversed. The first is common and unremarkable, since people rarely abandon a belief after a single encounter with contrary evidence. Only the second would justify the conclusion that correcting is counterproductive, and it is the second that the evidence has failed to find with any regularity.

This does not mean that correction is a cure. Its effects often fade over weeks, so that people drift back towards the belief they were talked out of, and accepting that a particular claim is false does not necessarily change the attitudes the claim was used to support. A voter may concede that a politician's statistic was wrong and still admire the politician exactly as much. These are serious limits, but they are limits of a different kind. They call for corrections that are repeated, that offer an alternative explanation rather than a bare denial, and that are not expected to carry more weight than a single fact can bear. They do not call for silence.

The history of the backfire effect is thus a small lesson about the life of findings as well as about belief. A striking result, especially one that confirms what people already suspect, can travel much faster than the slower work of checking it, and the effort to correct a mistaken finding meets the same ordinary resistance, though not reversal, that greets any correction.

options.A: shows that the larger studies described in paragraph 2 were mistaken about how people respond to corrections.
options.B: is an example of the backfire effect, since the correction has failed to weaken the belief at all.
options.C: demonstrates that people are perfectly unresponsive to evidence whenever a belief is tied to their loyalties.
options.D: offers no support for the view that correcting a false belief is likely to do more harm than good.

passage: Among the arguments made for nuclear deterrence, the strongest is also the simplest: when two states can each destroy the other, neither can hope to gain from a general war, and so neither starts one. Whatever its moral costs, a balance of terror of this kind has a claim to have kept the largest powers from fighting each other directly for a long time. But the logic that makes the largest war unthinkable may make smaller ones more thinkable, and this possibility, sometimes called the stability-instability paradox, deserves more attention than the reassuring half of the argument usually receives.

The reasoning runs as follows. If both sides are confident that neither will ever risk a nuclear exchange, then each can assume that a limited clash, whether a border skirmish, a proxy war or a raid by irregular forces, will stay limited. The fear that once restrained such ventures, the fear that they might spiral into catastrophe, is weakened precisely by the confidence that catastrophe will be avoided. Stability at the top of the ladder of escalation thus loosens the rungs near the bottom. A state that would never dare a full invasion may feel free to probe, provoke and nibble, reasoning that its opponent will not answer with anything that could lead to the unthinkable.

It is important to be precise about what this claims. It does not say that nuclear weapons cause small wars, which have many causes and were common long before such weapons existed. It says only that mutual deterrence can lower the perceived risk of low-level aggression and so remove one brake on it. Nor does the paradox operate automatically. Its force depends on how confident each side is that escalation can be controlled. Where leaders doubt that a skirmish can be kept small, the old fear returns, and with it some of the old caution.

The implication is uncomfortable for those who credit deterrence with keeping the peace. What deterrence may secure is not peace in general but the absence of one particular kind of war, while the violence that remains is pushed downward and outward, into contested borderlands and into the hands of proxies. That is no small achievement, given what the alternative might be, and nothing in the paradox implies that the world would be safer if the largest powers could once again contemplate fighting each other directly. But the achievement should be described accurately. A system that prevents catastrophe partly by making lesser conflicts safer to start is not a system of peace; it is a way of choosing which wars will be fought.

options.A: The author regards nuclear deterrence as a failure, since it has not succeeded in removing organised violence between rival states.
options.B: Small wars in the nuclear age are caused mainly by the confidence that mutual deterrence gives to the leaders of rival nuclear-armed states.
options.C: The paradox shows that the largest powers have in fact become more willing to fight each other directly once both are armed.
options.D: Where leaders doubt that clashes can be contained, deterrence is likely to weaken restraint on low-level aggression less than where they are confident of control.

passage: Debates about privacy in the age of large data sets usually begin from an image of ownership. Each person, on this view, holds a store of information about themselves, and the moral question is whether that information is taken with or without their permission. Hence the enormous weight placed on consent: the checkbox, the privacy notice, the setting that lets a user decline to share. If people are told what will happen to their data and agree to it, the transaction is treated as legitimate, and if they refuse, they are thought to have protected themselves.

The difficulty is that much personal information is not individual in the way the image assumes. A person who uploads their contact list discloses the names and numbers of people who agreed to nothing. Someone who submits a sample to a genetic testing service reveals facts about parents, siblings and cousins, some of whom may not know the test was taken. More subtly, when enough people share information about their habits, a system can learn the patterns that link one trait to another, and then infer those traits in people who shared nothing at all. A person who declines to disclose, say, a health condition may find that it has been estimated, with fair accuracy, from purchases and movements that resemble those of people who did disclose it.

One might reply that the refuser has still kept their own data, and that what others choose to reveal is their own affair. But this misses what the refuser was trying to protect. Nobody declines to share a fact for the sake of a particular row in a database; they decline because they do not want the fact known. If it can be known anyway, through the choices of others, then the refusal has secured very little, and the consent framework, which places the whole burden of protection on individual decisions, has quietly ceased to describe what is actually happening.

This does not make individual consent worthless. Being asked still matters, and a person who is deceived about how their information will be used has been wronged in a way that the collective character of data does not erase. The point is that consent cannot carry the load it has been given. Privacy behaves in part like clean air or quiet streets: a condition that each person's conduct affects for others, and that no one can secure for themselves by private choice alone. Protecting it therefore requires rules about what may be inferred and done, not merely about who has clicked agree.

options.A: Systems that infer traits from shared data become steadily more accurate as more people choose to disclose those traits.
options.B: Traits inferred about non-sharers from others' data prove so unreliable that they seldom reveal what a refuser meant to hide.
options.C: Many people who upload their contact lists do not realise that they are disclosing information about other people.
options.D: Deceiving people about how their information will be used remains a serious wrong even when the data involved is collective.

passage: The demonstration is by now familiar. Two groups are offered the same treatment, described in two ways: to one group as leaving ninety in a hundred patients alive after a year, to the other as seeing ten in a hundred die. The numbers are identical, yet the first description reliably attracts more support than the second. Since the treatment does not differ, the argument runs, a rational agent should not respond to the difference in wording, and the fact that people do respond is evidence that their preferences are shaped by presentation rather than substance. The principle appealed to, that logically equivalent descriptions should produce the same choice, has seemed so obvious that few have thought it needed defending.

Yet the principle is less obvious than it looks once we remember that descriptions do not fall from the sky. Somebody chooses them, and the choice is rarely arbitrary. A doctor who believes a treatment is worth trying tends, without any intent to manipulate, to speak of the patients it saves; a doctor with doubts more naturally mentions those it fails. Speakers also tend to describe a quantity in terms of the reference point from which it has moved: a glass that was full and has been partly drunk is more often called half empty than half full. If such regularities hold, then the frame carries information that the bare numbers do not, and a listener who draws an inference from it is not being swayed by mere wording. She is reading what the speaker's choice of words reveals, much as she would read an emphasis or a pause.

On this view, many framing effects are better described as sensitivity to implicit information than as failures of logic, and the experimenter who insists on equivalence has mistaken the logic of sentences for the logic of conversation. The equivalence holds between the propositions; it does not hold between the acts of uttering them, because those acts tell the hearer different things about the speaker. Participants who bring their ordinary conversational competence into the laboratory are, in a sense, being too reasonable for the experiment's purposes.

This rehabilitation should not be pushed too far. When experiments go to some lengths to make the frame visibly arbitrary, for example by assigning descriptions by an evident coin toss or by presenting both descriptions together, the inference from frame to speaker has nothing to work on, and a rational participant should set it aside. Effects in such conditions are often smaller, which is what the information account predicts, but they do not always vanish. Some residue seems to reflect the plain pull of words such as 'die' and 'lose', a reaction that would survive any amount of reflection about speakers. The information account explains a good deal of the phenomenon; it does not explain all of it.

What follows is a more discriminating verdict than either side usually offers. Whether responsiveness to a frame is a lapse depends on whether, in the situation at hand, the frame was a signal. Outside the laboratory it usually is, which is why habits formed in conversation are worth having. The danger lies precisely in that usefulness. A listener who reasonably treats frames as informative can be exploited by a speaker who knows the convention and chooses a frame to suggest a recommendation he would not dare to state outright. The fault in such cases lies less with the listener's inference than with the speaker's abuse of a norm that ordinarily makes the inference sound.

options.A: descriptions are chosen by speakers, and the choice often reveals something about what the speaker knows or believes.
options.B: descriptions are imposed by people in authority, so that listeners seldom feel able to question the way they are put.
options.C: descriptions used in experiments are carefully designed by researchers so that each pair is exactly equivalent.
options.D: descriptions take on their meaning only once the listener already knows the numbers that they are describing.

passage: Few kinds of article travel as easily as the list of untranslatable words. A language is said to possess a single word for the particular light that falls through leaves, another for the guilty pleasure of buying books one will never read, a third for the melancholy of a Sunday evening, and the reader is invited to marvel that English, or whatever language the list happens to be written in, has nothing to match them. The lists are charming, and most of the words in them are real. What is doubtful is the conclusion they are usually taken to support: that the speakers of a language without such a word cannot quite have the experience it names, or that a vocabulary is a window onto a national soul.

Look at what the lists actually demonstrate. Each entry pairs a foreign word with a sentence or two of English explaining it, and the explanation is usually clear enough that the reader recognises the experience at once, often with a small shock of familiarity. The list, in other words, translates every word it calls untranslatable. What it shows is not that a meaning cannot cross from one language to another but that one language packages in a single word what another expresses in a phrase. That is a fact about how vocabularies happen to be divided up, and it tells us very little about what their speakers are able to think or feel. Every language lacks single words for countless things its speakers understand perfectly well.

This is not to say that nothing is lost when such a word is carried across. A single word is easy to reach for; a phrase is not. A word that ordinary speakers use daily carries the weight of all those uses, along with a register, a sound and a set of associations that no paraphrase reproduces. The very existence of the word suggests that a community has found the experience worth naming, and that fact is itself a small piece of cultural information. For a translator working on a poem, where sound and compression matter as much as sense, these losses are real and constant, and no amount of explanation in a footnote restores them.

But the losses are of degree, not of kind, and they are not peculiar to exotic words. They occur whenever any word is rendered by another, and even within a single language, where no two synonyms carry quite the same associations. Seen this way, the romance of the untranslatable flatters the reader, who feels worldly for knowing the rare word, and it encourages a picture of cultures as sealed rooms whose inhabitants can only be gazed at, never understood. The more modest and more accurate lesson is that translation is always possible and never complete, and that its difficulties lie less in the dictionary than in everything a word drags along with it.

options.A: include many words that are invented or exaggerated and that ordinary speakers of the original language never use.
options.B: explain each supposedly untranslatable word clearly in the very language said to have no equivalent for it.
options.C: show that speakers of every language share exactly the same experiences, which makes the special words unnecessary.
options.D: present foreign words without examples, so that readers never learn how the words are used in daily speech.

options.B: the process by which a translator compresses a long explanation of a word into a brief footnote.

options.D: the way one language bundles into a single word a meaning that another language spreads across several words.

passage: Most people in the modern West assume that a name is a fixed possession, given once at birth and carried, with perhaps one change at marriage, until death. The assumption is so deep that we rarely notice it is an assumption at all, yet in a wide range of societies a person's name has been expected to change over a lifetime, and one of the commonest occasions for the change is the birth of a child. When a man becomes known as the father of his first child, or a woman as the mother of hers, anthropologists speak of teknonymy: naming a parent through the offspring. The Arabic custom of addressing a man as Abu, 'father of', followed by the name of his eldest son, is perhaps the most familiar instance, but the practice in various forms has been recorded on several continents.

It is tempting to read teknonymy as a simple sign that children are prized, and there is something in this. But the more interesting point is what the custom reveals about how such societies understand a person. In a system of fixed names, identity is treated as something an individual owns from the start, and relationships are added to it later, like rooms built onto a house. In a teknonymous system the order is reversed: a person becomes fully visible in social life only by standing in a relationship; the new name announces not that the individual has changed but that their position in a web of kin has changed. One is addressed less as a self than as a point where generations meet.

This also explains a feature that puzzles outsiders. In some communities it becomes mildly rude to use the old personal name of an adult who has a child, much as it would be odd for us to call a judge by a childhood nickname in court. The personal name has not been forbidden; it has simply been outranked by a title that carries more social information. Where the practice extends further, so that a grandparent is named after a grandchild, a person's name can track their rise through the generations, and the most senior people come to be known almost entirely through their descendants.

None of this should be romanticised, for a system that names people through their children can be hard on those who have none, who may remain, in the language of address, permanently junior. Nor is the Western fixed name as individualistic as it looks, since a surname itself announces a lineage. The contrast is one of emphasis rather than of kind, but the emphasis matters. To change a person's name at the birth of a child is to state, every time that person is greeted, that adulthood is not a private achievement but a place in a sequence.

passage: Among the ideas that have shaped thinking about growth and fairness, few have travelled as far as the proposal, first advanced in the middle of the twentieth century, that inequality traces an inverted U as an economy develops. In the early stages, the argument ran, inequality rises as some workers move from a poor and fairly equal agricultural sector into a richer and more unequal industrial one; later, as most of the workforce has made the move and the new urban classes gain education and political voice, inequality falls again. The idea was offered tentatively, on the strength of a handful of national histories, but it hardened over the following decades into something closer to a law.

The mechanism at its core is sound as far as it goes. If a population is divided between two sectors with different average incomes, moving people from the lower to the higher will, by simple arithmetic, widen overall inequality for a time and then narrow it once the shift is largely complete. What does not follow is that this arithmetic governs the course of inequality in real economies, where it competes with many other forces. As data accumulated for more countries and longer periods, the curve proved elusive. Some economies grew rapidly while inequality stayed flat or fell; others saw inequality rise again after a long decline, a second upswing for which the original story had no room.

The damage done by treating the curve as a law was not mainly to economic theory. It was to policy. If rising inequality is a natural stage of development that growth will itself reverse, then governments in poor countries can be told to tolerate it, and governments in rich ones can be assured that any widening is a passing disturbance. Both lessons encourage waiting. Yet in the historical episodes that did show a decline, the fall rarely arrived on its own. It came alongside the spread of public schooling, the growth of organised labour, progressive taxation and, in several cases, the destruction of concentrated wealth by war and inflation.

A better reading treats the inverted U not as a path that development follows but as a record of what happened in some places when particular structural shifts met particular political choices. Read that way, the curve still teaches something, chiefly that the movement of people between sectors matters for how incomes are distributed. What it cannot do is assure a government that inequality will take care of itself.

options.A: having been produced by measures that governments adopted deliberately in order to reduce inequality.
options.B: having been caused chiefly by the destruction of concentrated wealth in wars and periods of high inflation.
options.C: having involved more than the shift of workers between sectors, since the fall usually came together with other changes.
options.D: evidence that the inverted U never actually described the experience of any economy at all.
